title: Donepezil: Cholinesterase Inhibition Without a Dementia Cure
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
bottomLine: Donepezil is a cholinesterase inhibitor used for symptomatic treatment of Alzheimer disease. It may modestly support cognition/function but does not reverse neurodegeneration; bradycardia, syncope, GI effects, weight loss, and cholinergic toxicity are priority nursing concerns.
recognize: Nausea, diarrhea, anorexia, and weight loss can occur.
Slow pulse, dizziness, falls, or syncope may reflect vagotonic effects.
priorities: Review pulse, fall/syncope history, weight trend, and interacting drugs that slow heart rate.
Escalate symptomatic bradycardia, GI bleeding, severe vomiting, or new seizure/syncope.
assessMonitor: Monitor cognition/function trend, pulse, weight, hydration, GI tolerance, falls, and medication adherence.
interventions: Administer consistently and reinforce realistic expectations that benefit is symptomatic, not curative.
medicationSafety: Use caution with conduction disease and other bradycardic drugs.
Alert perioperative teams because cholinesterase inhibition can interact with neuromuscular-blocking agents.
teaching: Report fainting, slow pulse, major appetite/weight loss, or GI bleeding; do not expect the drug to cure dementia.
delegationScope: PNs may administer and monitor response/adverse effects; new syncope or major cognitive/functional decline requires RN/provider evaluation.
examTrap: Assuming improved alertness means Alzheimer disease has been reversed.
oneLinePearl: Donepezil may support function; monitor the gut, weight, pulse, and falls.

title: Memantine: NMDA Antagonism for Moderate-to-Severe Alzheimer Disease
bottomLine: Memantine is an NMDA-receptor antagonist used for moderate-to-severe Alzheimer disease. It is not treatment for acute delirium; dizziness, confusion, constipation, renal function, and medication interactions matter.
recognize: Dizziness, headache, confusion, or constipation may occur.
Abrupt acute confusion should trigger delirium evaluation rather than automatic dose escalation.
priorities: Review renal function and current cognitive baseline.
Evaluate new acute confusion for infection, medications, metabolic problems, pain, or other delirium causes.
assessMonitor: Monitor cognition/function trend, dizziness/falls, bowel pattern, renal status, and adherence.
interventions: Administer as prescribed and distinguish chronic dementia symptoms from new acute mental-status change.
medicationSafety: Renal impairment can increase exposure.
Urine-alkalinizing conditions/drugs can reduce clearance and raise memantine exposure.
teaching: Report sudden confusion or major behavior change; those findings may represent illness rather than dementia progression.
delegationScope: PNs may administer and monitor; acute mental-status change requires escalation for assessment.
examTrap: Using memantine as the answer for a sudden overnight change in cognition.
oneLinePearl: Memantine is chronic dementia therapy—not an acute delirium fix.

title: Galantamine: Cholinergic Dementia Therapy and Bradycardia Risk
bottomLine: Galantamine is a cholinesterase inhibitor used for mild-to-moderate Alzheimer dementia. GI intolerance, weight loss, bradycardia/syncope, renal/hepatic considerations, and medication adherence are central nursing safety issues.
recognize: Nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, and appetite loss can reduce weight and hydration.
Bradycardia or syncope may increase fall risk.
priorities: Review pulse, weight, hydration, renal/hepatic context, and fall history.
Escalate syncope, severe GI loss, or GI bleeding.
assessMonitor: Monitor cognition/function, pulse, weight, GI tolerance, hydration, and falls.
interventions: Administer with appropriate food/fluid instructions for the formulation and reinforce adherence.
medicationSafety: Do not restart a long-interrupted regimen at the prior high dose without prescriber guidance.
Use caution with other cholinergic or bradycardic agents.
teaching: Report fainting, persistent GI symptoms, or meaningful weight loss.
delegationScope: PNs may administer and trend tolerance; syncope or acute decline requires RN/provider escalation.
examTrap: Treating severe vomiting and weight loss as acceptable evidence that the medicine is working.
oneLinePearl: Galantamine helps symptoms only if the patient can safely tolerate the cholinergic effects.

title: Carbidopa/Levodopa: Motor Benefit, Wearing-Off, and Safety
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
bottomLine: Carbidopa/levodopa replaces dopamine precursor activity for Parkinson motor symptoms. Nursing priorities are consistent timing, orthostatic/fall safety, dyskinesia and hallucination recognition, wearing-off patterns, and avoiding abrupt withdrawal.
recognize: Improved rigidity/bradykinesia should be distinguished from dyskinesia caused by excess dopaminergic effect.
End-of-dose wearing off can present as predictable return of motor symptoms.
priorities: Give doses on schedule and document relation of symptoms to dose timing.
Escalate severe hallucinations, syncope, new dyskinesia, or abrupt functional decline.
assessMonitor: Monitor mobility, orthostatic symptoms, dyskinesia, hallucinations, sleepiness, falls, and meal/iron timing issues.
interventions: Maintain exact formulation/timing and support fall precautions during medication transitions.
medicationSafety: Do not stop abruptly; severe rigidity, fever, confusion, and autonomic instability can occur with sudden dopaminergic withdrawal.
High-protein meals and iron can alter absorption in some patients; follow individualized timing instructions.
redFlags: Fever with severe rigidity after missed/stopped doses
teaching: Take on schedule and report wearing-off, involuntary movements, hallucinations, or sudden sleep episodes.
delegationScope: PNs may administer and observe response; medication adjustment remains prescriber-directed.
examTrap: Withholding a time-critical Parkinson dose because the patient is temporarily NPO without escalating for an alternative plan.
oneLinePearl: For levodopa, timing is therapy—late doses can look like sudden neurologic decline.

title: Entacapone: Extending Levodopa and Intensifying Its Adverse Effects
bottomLine: Entacapone is a COMT inhibitor used with levodopa/carbidopa to reduce end-of-dose wearing off. Because it increases levodopa exposure, dyskinesia, orthostasis, hallucinations, and somnolence may worsen.
recognize: More dyskinesia after starting entacapone can reflect increased levodopa effect.
Orange-brown urine discoloration can occur and is generally benign.
priorities: Link symptom changes to levodopa/entacapone timing.
Escalate troublesome dyskinesia, hallucinations, syncope, or severe diarrhea.
assessMonitor: Monitor wearing-off duration, dyskinesia, BP, hallucinations, sleepiness, diarrhea, and mobility.
interventions: Administer with each prescribed levodopa/carbidopa dose according to regimen.
medicationSafety: It is adjunct therapy, not standalone Parkinson treatment.
Do not abruptly stop the overall dopaminergic regimen without guidance.
teaching: Harmless urine discoloration differs from blood in urine; report severe diarrhea, hallucinations, or involuntary movements.
delegationScope: PNs may administer and monitor; regimen changes require prescriber review.
examTrap: Adding entacapone and ignoring new dyskinesia because the Parkinson symptoms seem better.
oneLinePearl: Entacapone makes levodopa last longer—and can make levodopa side effects stronger.

title: Pramipexole: Dopamine Agonist, Sleep Attacks, and Impulse-Control Risk
bottomLine: Pramipexole is a dopamine agonist used for Parkinson disease and selected restless-legs indications. Sudden sleep, orthostatic hypotension, hallucinations, edema, impulse-control disorders, renal accumulation, and withdrawal effects require active monitoring.
recognize: New compulsive gambling, shopping, eating, or sexual behavior can be medication related.
Patients may fall asleep during activities without much warning.
priorities: Assess daytime sleepiness, orthostasis, hallucinations, behavior change, and renal function.
Escalate dangerous sleep attacks, psychosis, or severe impulse-control behavior.
assessMonitor: Monitor BP/falls, sleepiness, hallucinations, edema, impulse-control symptoms, and renal status.
interventions: Implement fall/driving safety and report behavior changes promptly.
medicationSafety: Renal impairment affects dosing.
Do not stop suddenly without a taper plan because withdrawal symptoms can occur.
teaching: Family/caregivers should report new compulsive behaviors or hallucinations; avoid driving if sudden sleepiness occurs.
delegationScope: PNs may administer and monitor; dose/taper decisions remain prescriber-directed.
examTrap: Treating sudden compulsive gambling as a purely social problem without considering dopamine-agonist therapy.
oneLinePearl: With pramipexole, monitor sleep, pressure, perception, and impulses.

title: Levetiracetam: Seizure Control and Behavioral Safety
bottomLine: Levetiracetam is an antiseizure medication with few pharmacokinetic interactions, but somnolence, dizziness, behavioral change, mood symptoms, suicidality, and renal accumulation are key safety concerns. Abrupt discontinuation can provoke seizures.
recognize: Irritability, aggression, depression, agitation, or suicidal thinking can emerge after initiation or dose change.
Sedation and dizziness increase fall/injury risk.
priorities: Review seizure pattern, mood/behavior, renal function, adherence, and fall risk.
Escalate suicidality, severe aggression, status epilepticus, or serious rash/hypersensitivity.
assessMonitor: Monitor seizure frequency, behavior/mood, sedation, renal function, and adherence.
interventions: Maintain seizure precautions and consistent administration.
medicationSafety: Renal dosing may be required.
Do not stop abruptly unless emergency specialist guidance directs otherwise.
teaching: Report new mood or behavior changes promptly and do not stop the medicine suddenly.
delegationScope: PNs may administer and monitor; acute seizure deterioration or major psychiatric change requires escalation.
examTrap: Assuming an antiseizure drug with few interactions has no serious behavioral adverse effects.

title: Gabapentin: Neuropathic Pain, Renal Dosing, and Respiratory Sedation
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
bottomLine: Gabapentin is used for postherpetic neuralgia and as adjunctive seizure therapy. Sedation, dizziness, ataxia, renal accumulation, and respiratory depression—especially with opioids or other CNS depressants—are the main nursing safety issues.
recognize: New somnolence, slowed breathing, or unsteady gait is more concerning when opioids/sedatives are also present.
Reduced renal clearance can cause drug accumulation.
priorities: Review renal function, CNS depressants, respiratory status, falls, and indication.
Escalate excessive sedation, respiratory depression, or suicidality.
assessMonitor: Monitor pain/seizure response, sedation, respiratory status, gait/falls, edema, mood, and renal function.
interventions: Use fall precautions and coordinate dose review when kidney function worsens.
medicationSafety: Avoid abrupt discontinuation after regular use; taper as directed.
Antacids can affect absorption timing depending on product; follow label/pharmacy instructions.
teaching: Avoid unapproved alcohol/sedative combinations and report excessive sleepiness or breathing difficulty.
delegationScope: PNs may administer and monitor; respiratory depression requires immediate escalation.
examTrap: Treating profound sedation in a patient taking gabapentin plus opioids as an expected harmless effect.
oneLinePearl: Gabapentin plus kidney disease or CNS depressants can turn sleepiness into a safety emergency.

title: Pregabalin: Neuropathic Pain, Edema, and CNS-Depressant Risk
bottomLine: Pregabalin is used for several neuropathic-pain syndromes and adjunctive seizure therapy and is a controlled substance. Dizziness, somnolence, edema/weight gain, angioedema, renal accumulation, and respiratory depression with CNS depressants are major nursing concerns.
recognize: Peripheral edema and weight gain may worsen functional or heart-failure concerns.
Facial/tongue swelling can signal angioedema.
priorities: Review renal function, opioid/sedative use, edema, respiratory status, and fall risk.
Escalate angioedema or respiratory depression immediately.
assessMonitor: Monitor pain/seizure response, sedation, respiration, edema/weight, renal function, mood, and falls.
interventions: Use fall precautions and reinforce secure medication handling.
medicationSafety: Dose adjustment is required with reduced renal function.
Taper rather than stop abruptly after regular therapy.
teaching: Do not share medication; report swelling, breathing difficulty, or severe sleepiness.
delegationScope: PNs may administer and monitor; airway or respiratory compromise requires emergency escalation.
examTrap: Ignoring new facial swelling because peripheral edema is already listed as a common adverse effect.
oneLinePearl: Pregabalin can swell the legs—but swelling the airway is an emergency.

title: Buspirone: Scheduled Anxiolysis, Not PRN Panic Rescue
bottomLine: Buspirone is a non-benzodiazepine anxiolytic generally used as scheduled therapy; benefit develops over time, so it is not a rapid PRN rescue drug for an acute panic episode. Dizziness and serotonergic/MAOI interactions are key safety issues.
recognize: Dizziness, nausea, headache, or nervousness can occur early.
Improvement is gradual rather than immediate after one dose.
priorities: Verify scheduled use, interacting serotonergic drugs/MAOIs, and adherence.
Escalate severe serotonin-toxicity symptoms or syncope.
assessMonitor: Monitor anxiety/function over time, dizziness/falls, adherence, and interaction symptoms.
interventions: Administer consistently with respect to food because food changes bioavailability; use the same pattern each day.
medicationSafety: Do not combine with MAO inhibitors in prohibited timing windows.
Do not substitute for benzodiazepine-withdrawal management or acute emergency sedation.
teaching: Take consistently; do not judge effectiveness after one dose or use it as an instant panic-relief medication.
delegationScope: PNs may administer and monitor; acute psychiatric danger or serotonin toxicity requires escalation.
examTrap: Giving buspirone PRN and expecting it to stop a panic attack within minutes.
oneLinePearl: Buspirone works by consistency, not immediacy.
